content: Cough is a common symptom that frequently leads parents to seek medical attention for their children. In certain clinical settings, the most prevalent cause of chronic wet cough in children, defined as a cough lasting more than four weeks, is protracted bacterial bronchitis (PBB). However, other more serious conditions can also present with similar symptoms. Prompt and effective treatment of chronic wet or productive cough is essential, as it can significantly improve both the quality of life and clinical outcomes for affected children. Current international guidelines recommend a course of antibiotics as the first-line treatment in cases where there are no signs or symptoms pointing to an alternative diagnosis. This review aimed to evaluate the evidence supporting this recommendation. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of antibiotics in treating children with prolonged wet cough, excluding those with bronchiectasis or other known underlying respiratory illnesses. Additionally, the review sought to evaluate the potential risks of adverse events associated with antibiotic use in this population. An updated search was conducted, covering studies from 2008 onwards, using multiple databases and sources, including the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, trial registries, review articles, and reference lists of relevant studies. The most recent search was completed in September 2017. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared antibiotics to a placebo or control group in children with chronic wet cough. Cluster and cross-over trials were excluded. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers selected, extracted, and assessed the data for inclusion, and study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. Data were analyzed on an intention-to-treat basis. Three studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. Two of these studies were included in a previous review, while one was newly identified. The older studies were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias, whereas the newly included study was assessed as having a low risk of bias. The studies varied in terms of treatment duration (ranging from 7 to 14 days) and the antibiotics used (two studies used amoxicillin/clavulanate, and one used erythromycin). A total of 190 children were included in the meta-analyses, with 171 completing the studies. The mean ages of participants ranged from 21 months to six years. The meta-analysis of all three trials (190 children) demonstrated that antibiotic treatment significantly reduced the proportion of children who were not cured at follow-up, which was the primary outcome measure. The odds ratio (OR) was 0.15 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.07 to 0.31), corresponding to a number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) of 3 (95% CI 2 to 4). There was no significant heterogeneity among the studies (I² = 0% for both fixed-effect and random-effects models). Two of the older trials (125 children) also assessed the progression of illness, defined as the need for additional antibiotics. The results showed that the progression of illness was significantly lower in the antibiotic group, with an OR of 0.10 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.34) and an NNTB of 4 (95% CI 3 to 5). All three trials (190 children) reported adverse events. However, the incidence of adverse events was not significantly higher in the antibiotic group compared to the control group (OR 1.88, 95% CI 0.62 to 5.69). The quality of evidence, as assessed using the GRADE system, was rated as moderate for all outcome measures except for adverse events, which were rated as low quality. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that antibiotics are effective in treating children with chronic wet cough lasting more than four weeks, with an NNTB of three. However, antibiotics are associated with potential adverse effects, and this review highlighted uncertainty regarding the risk of increased adverse events in this context. The inclusion of a more robust study in this review has strengthened the findings of the previous Cochrane review and its conclusions.
